facts.text: Microcopy is every word in a product that is not body content: the buttons, the field labels, the placeholder hints, the validation messages, the empty states, the toasts, the modal titles, the 404 pages. Collectively, microcopy is the voice of the product.

facets.title: 1. The "verb the noun" rule for buttons

facts.text: Buttons should describe the action they perform. The canonical shape is verb + noun.
Echo the action's verb in destructive confirmations. If the dialog asks "Delete this project?", the destructive button says "Delete project," not "Yes" or "Confirm."

facets.title: 2. The "what you can do here" rule for empty states

facts.text: Name the absence (one short line).
Tell the user what this surface is for.
Give them the next action (with a button when possible).
Weak: "No items." Stronger: "No saved designs yet / This is where your saved email designs will live. / [Create your first design]"

facets.title: 3. The "be specific" rule for error and validation messages

facts.text: Nielsen Norman Group's canonical four-part guideline:
State what went wrong in plain language.
Explain why, if useful.
Tell the user how to fix it.
Don't blame the user.
Never use exclamation points in failure messages.

facets.title: 4. The match-the-verb rule for destructive confirmations

facts.text: Avoid: "Are you sure?" as a title. "OK" / "Cancel" as button pair. "Yes" / "No" as button pair.

facets.title: 5. Tooltips, helper text, placeholders — distinct uses

facts.text: Anti-pattern: Placeholder as label. When the user starts typing, the label vanishes.

facets.title: 6. Toasts, banners, modals — match severity to surface

facts.text: Toast copy is the shortest writing in the product. Single word or short verb-noun phrase. Past-tense for completed actions: "Saved" not "Your changes were saved successfully."

facets.title: 7. Consent, opt-in, opt-out — symmetry of choice

facts.text: The path to the more privacy-protective choice must not be harder than the path to the less privacy-protective choice.
NN/g's four dimensions to calibrate tone:
Funny vs Serious - billing errors are serious; an empty state for a hobby app can be playful.
Formal vs Casual - enterprise tools lean formal, consumer apps lean casual.
When to drop humor entirely: anything involving money, security, or privacy; anything destructive or irreversible; anything during an outage or sign-in failure.
"Submit" - almost never the right word.
Placeholder-as-label - field with no visible, persistent label.
Apologetic empty states - "Oh no, you have no projects yet!"
"Are you sure?" as the only confirmation question - vague.
Yes/No buttons on confirmation dialogs - forces the user to re-read the title.
Exclamation points in error messages.
Pre-checked marketing opt-ins.
